articles.content: If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June, you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike. If you want a larger display, Amazon and Best Buy are also taking $300 off the otherwise identical 15-inch model with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, dropping it to $1,199. Its faster chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage make it better suited for multitasking and creative work in apps like Photoshop and Premiere. You also get a higher-resolution display, better speakers, a backlit keyboard that makes typing in the dark easier, and faster ports. Plus, its sharper webcam supports Apple’s Center Stage feature, which automatically adjusts the framing to keep you in view during video calls. Of course, the Air can’t match the performance or higher-end displays you can get with a MacBook Pro, whether you opt for an M5 model, the newer M5 Pro model with a PROLED XDR Display, or one of the M6-powered machines. A Pro may be worth the extra money if you regularly edit video or work on more demanding creative projects. But if you mostly need a laptop for work, browsing, and occasional photo or video editing, the M5 Air is more than capable. Read our M5-powered MacBook Air review.

articles.title: L’Anse Creuse Unified outlasts Grosse Pointe North; Troy upends De La Salle in OT
articles.content: Macomb L’Anse Creuse Unified continued one of its best starts in program history. Unified only trailed once Friday before outlasting Grosse Pointe North 7-5 in a Macomb Area Conference White Division clash at Fraser’s Big Boy Arena. Ethan Shirilla scored a short-handed goal with 3:48 left in the second period which gave Unified a 6-4 lead and proved to be the game-winning goal to help lift Unified to a 7-1-0 overall record and 2-1 in conference play. While leading goal scorer Joey Tringali was left off the scoreboard for the first time this season, he still had an impact of LCU after drawing plenty of attention and drawing three assists in the game. Shirilla led LCU with three goals and an assist and Rocco Abbate added two goals and an assist for L’Anse Creuse Unified. Blake Dove had a goal and an assist, Dominic Percy scored a goal, Easton Paquette drew two assists while Adam Gutierrez picked up a single helper to aid LCU’s winning effort. AJ Maurin finished with 30 saves for LCU. Charlie Mueller staked Grosse Pointe North (2-4-0, 1-2) to a 1-0 lead just 29 seconds into the contest only to see LCU’s Percy convert on a power play with 10:10 remaining in the opening period to tie the game at 1-1. LCU went ahead twice more with Grosse Pointe North tying the game two other times. Abbate’s goal with 13 seconds left in the third period gave Unified a 3-2 lead and the team never trailed again. Mueller got a stick in all five of Grosse Pointe North’s goals by finishing with four goals and an assist. Ben Clor scored the fifth goal late in the third period, Andrew Phillips drew four assists, Brandon Shock had two helpers, Aidan Burney picked up two assists and Andrew Phillips and Logan Perry had a single assist for the Norsemen. Ben Bugeja finished with 34 saves for Grosse Pointe North. Alex Chrobak stuck the puck into the back of the net with 4:26 left in overtime Friday following a feed from Noah Scullin which gave Troy United a thrilling 5-4 non-league triumph over Warren De La Salle. The game was tied 3-3 after the third period, as Troy’s Bryce Czartoryski scored for United (4-3-0) with 8:47 left in regulation, while John McKay netted an equalizer with just 2:22 left to tie the game for De La Salle (2-2-0) and force overtime. Czartoryski finished with two goals and an assist and Chrobak added two goals for the winners. Yomata Kuwabara also scored, while Kaiser Ascenio, Eston Smith, Scullin, Jeremiah Sillers and Dominik Blackwell had single assists for Troy. Noah Dumas finished with 25 saves in 54:34 of action to gain the win in goal for United. Keegan Taylor had three goals with an assist for De La Salle. McKay added a goal and an assist, while Luke Sirko and Landen Taylor also drew assists for the Pilots, who dropped their second overtime game of the season. Rowan Gulewicz picked up 30 saves for De La Salle despite the loss.

articles.title: Something special: Colorado-bound Annie Hrabovsky on course to become Macomb County’s all-time best distance runner
articles.content: Annie Hrabovsky didn’t enter high school expecting to be great. She just wanted to excel. It’s safe to say that the current Romeo High School senior is both. Not only has she became one of her school’s all-time distance runners coupling cross country and track, but she is perhaps the top distance ace in Macomb County history – and with two-thirds of her senior year still to go. “When I was a freshman, I just wanted to go out there and compete. We had some really good runners and we knew we had a very good team,” recalled Hrabovsky. Romeo was the Division 1 team state champion in 2023 and followed that up with another state title run in 2024. Last year, the Bulldogs were second while in 2026 the team still finished fourth even though they finished second at their regional. The Bulldogs have been one of the most dominant programs in cross country and track and field Macomb County has seen for the past two decades. Hrabovsky has developed quite a reputation of being the ultimate competitor, leading her team to countless championships and top 10 finishes along the way while earning her own share of medals between the two sports. Hrabovsky was contacted by numerous NCAA Division I and Division II schools over the past couple of years and recently committed and signed earlier this month with NCAA Division I University of Colorado to compete for the Buffaloes in the Big 12 Conference in the near future. Mike Bulsepp, Romeo’s distance coach in track and head cross country coach in the fall, knew Hrabovsky was going to make an impact. But at this level? “I would say that right now she is the best we’ve seen in Macomb County, especially in cross country,” he said. “She works so hard that at times we’ve had to tone her down (with training). We decided (last spring) to back her down from certain meets. But she has as great state meet last spring in track with two All-State finishes. In cross country, she missed several meets, but we knew she would come back near the end when the meets really mattered and she ended up fourth at the state meet. “I knew she was going to be tough,” he continued. “But what she has done over the years is truly (remarkable).” Hrabovsky entered Romeo’s hallways in 2023 already an established runner in her age group and quickly cemented herself as one of Romeo‘s top runners from the start. There have been no signs of her slowing down – although she did miss several meets last spring during track and field and several meets this fall during her senior season of cross country due to some nagging injuries. On the cross country trails, Hrabovsky finished in the top 11 at the Lower Peninsula Division 1 state finals all four years. She was fourth as a freshman (17:28.7), 11th as a sophomore (17:46.8), third as a junior (17:22.1) and fourth as a senior earlier this month at Michigan Speedway with one of her best finishes timewise, clocking 17:07.5. Not to mention all of the top 10 finishes at other championship-style invitationals, including Macomb County, Macomb Area Conference Red Division, regional meets and large all-star meets such as the Holly, Spartans, Portage, Lamplighter, Jackson invitationals and a host of others during the last four school years. This season after returning from a series of injuries – she didn’t race between the MHSAA Division 1 track and field finals in early June until October of this year in cross country – Hrabovsky was second at the Macomb County meet, first at the Columbus Country Park regional, fourth at the D-1 state meet while at the recent NXR Midwest Regionals down in Terre Haute, Ind., she finished a blistering third in 16:52.1, which lowered her school record by some three seconds. “I ran 16:55 last year at our league meet, but some people were saying that the course may have been a little short,” noted Hrabovsky, who qualified for NXN Nationals meet in Portland, Oregon, on Dec. 5. “I felt really good at the NXR (regionals) and I had my best time there.” While Hrabovsky competed at those Midwest and national meet under the Runners High club team, her 16:52.1 effort will still be counted in the school record books. That is also the fastest time ever recorded by a Macomb County female athlete in cross country. “I am going out there and I would love to finish maybe in the top 15,” said Hrabovsky. “There’s going to be some really good girls at that meet. I’m really looking forward to the competition.” In track and field, Hrabovsky sat out some key meets last spring but had another strong finish. She placed sixth in the 1,600 meters (4:58.83) and came back to place second in the 3,200 meters (10:25.4). She either owns the school record or is top five in the stance events for Romeo and is hoping to lower her times in those events next spring before she heads west to Boulder, Colorado, next summer. As a freshman in the spring of 2024, she was seventh in the 3,200 (10:42.42) while in 2025 as a sophomore she crossed fifth at state in the 3,200 (10:31.71). “I am looking forward to running in college,” noted Hrabovsky. “But I still have a lot of races to go before then. I hope I can go much faster in track, especially the (3,200). I hope I can do a lot better in the 1,600. I rarely ever race in the 800, but that’s okay unless they need me in a relay. “I just love being out there and competing,” she continued. “My whole family is runners and my siblings have run here or are running here right now. When I was in the eighth grade, our school record was Teresa Bongiovanni (in the early 2000s) and she ran 17:59. It’s become a lot more competitive (since then) and Romeo has had a lot of great runners over the years. We’ve had several girls run well under 18 minutes. We had three girls go (NCAA Division I) from last year’s team. “It’s that competitive. I’ve heard a lot about some of the great runners in Michigan (over the years) and I know how competitive it has become. I’m glad to be out there racing against great competition,” added Hrabovsky. The final prep chapters have yet to close for Romeo’s star runner. Following the NXN national meet, Hrabovsky will still have the indoor track and field circuit, plus her final year of outdoor high school track and field. “There’s still a lot of races coming up,” she added. “I know we’ll have a good team in track again and I hope I can help us win some more meets. Once we get to the (state finals),, I’m really hoping to lower my times in the (3,200) and even the (1,600) and see how fast I can go. We have a great coach in Coach Bulsepp and he always has us prepared to run our best at the big meets. I feel like that is a big reason for my success and the success of Romeo’s teams.”

Mamdani recovering after ‘successful’ Achilles surgery
articles.content: NEW YORK (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani is back at Gracie Mansion recovering after undergoing successful surgery on his Achilles tendon on Friday. Press Secretary Joe Calvello released a statement saying Mamdani's procedure began at 11:33 a.m. and concluded at 12:42 p.m., and called the surgery "successful," with the mayor expected to "make a full recovery." "He was discharged from the hospital and is now resting comfortably at Gracie Mansion. We are extremely grateful for the first-class care the Mayor received from the medical staff today. First Deputy Mayor Dean Fuleihan is leading day-to-day operations today," Calvello said in the statement. Mamdani said he tore his Achilles during a friendly game of soccer with the press corps last week. The mayor, who just recently turned 35, said he suffered a non-contact injury while running for a ball on the indoor turf in the second half. He admitted that he did not stretch before the game. Prior to the surgery, Mamdani admitted "I'm scared, it's my first surgery," but said, "I keep telling myself, Jayson Tatum did it, anything is possible."

ACLU seeks court order blocking Trump administration's efforts to unmask ICE critics on social media
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is abusing the grand jury process in an effort to unmask social media users anonymously criticizing its immigration enforcement tactics, civil rights attorneys claim in a federal court filing Friday. A federal class action, backed by the American Civil Liberties Union, seeks a court order enjoining the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security from conducting a “bad-faith investigation” that violates the anonymous individuals’ First Amendment free speech rights. The scope of the investigation remains a mystery, but the ACLU says government lawyers have issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas seeking to identify critics and provide their personal information to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement investigators. ACLU attorneys sued on behalf of four unnamed social media users, asking the district court in Washington to block subpoenas seeking account information for users of social media companies, including Meta, Bluesky and X, formerly known as Twitter. Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the ACLU case’s unsealing on Wednesday. Boasberg scheduled a Jan. 6 hearing for arguments on the ACLU’s request for a preliminary injunction against the government. The administration has until Dec. 14 to respond in writing to the ACLU’s allegations. Spokespeople for DHS and U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office in Washington didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Pirro, Attorney General Todd Blanche and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin are named as defendants in the ACLU’s lawsuit. ACLU lawyers say Pirro’s office has used the term “Investigation 18” to describe efforts to identify and obtain the personal information. “The investigation,” the ACLU says, “is a bad-faith fishing expedition initiated to gather intrusive intelligence and facilitate retaliation against dissenters.” The ACLU says its lawsuit in Washington is the “first systemic civil challenge, and the first case that will be litigated in public view, to the Trump administration’s abuse of grand jury unmasking subpoenas.” “The government is weaponizing the grand jury process to retaliate against people for expressing their political views online,” ACLU attorney Laura Moraff said in a statement. The ACLU argues that the subpoenas to social media platforms are part of a broader pattern of intimidation. DHS has sent hundreds of administrative subpoenas to tech companies in the past year to seek information about online ICE critics, the ACLU says. The civil rights organization says the Trump administration has shifted to using grand jury subpoenas — a more secretive process — after encountering pushback to the administrative subpoenas from users and tech companies. The ACLU lawsuit’s plaintiffs include a Bluesky user who wrote about an ICE-related shooting in New York by posting: “Burn ICE to the ground. Burn DHS to the ground. Salt the earth.” Another plaintiff is a college student whose posts on X included an expletive directed at DHS, ICE and Trump. “Defendants’ rampant use of subpoenas to unmask critics of the federal government is occurring against the backdrop of repeated suggestions that Defendants are building a database of dissenters,” ACLU lawyers wrote.

articles.description: Kenya cult leader found guilty of manslaughter of over 100 followers asked to starve to meet Jesus AP News Kenyan starvation cult leader guilty of manslaughter for 123 deaths in latest conviction Reuters Paul Mackenzie: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths BBC Kenyan cult leader in jail for 191 murders convicted over another 123 deaths Sky News Kenyan cult leader guilty of manslaughter more t
articles.content: NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie was on Friday found guilty of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers, the latest in a series of convictions against him for the deaths of hundreds of his followers. The founder and pastor of the Good News International Church was found guilty of asking his followers to fast to death in order to meet Jesus. He was convicted together with 29 of his followers, including his wife Rhoda Mumbua, at a trial in the coastal city of Mombasa. Authorities in 2023 uncovered more than 400 bodies in mass graves scattered across a vast ranch near Malindi town, where Mackenzie’s followers had relocated to evade scrutiny. Children were reportedly the first to succumb to the starvation. Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison on Nov. 7 for the murder of 191 people, including 190 children and one adult. He’s facing a series of trials on various charges reflecting different ways members of his organization died. He was also convicted on Wednesday of child cruelty and radicalization in a separate case. Mackenzie is due to be sentenced on the child cruelty and radicalization charges in December.

TWTS: Odds, ends, and other linguistic leftovers
articles.description: For everyone who had big Thanksgiving meals on Thursday, they may now be figuring out ways to use up the odds and ends in the fridge.
articles.content: After Thanksgiving, the refrigerator can become a collection of odds and ends: a little cranberry sauce, a few spoonfuls of mashed potatoes, and whatever else didn’t make it onto the dinner table. But the phrase "odds and ends" has a history of its own, and it may have started with just the ends."Odds and ends" dates back to the mid-1700s, referring to miscellaneous things, fragments, or remnants. Its predecessor, "odd ends," appears much earlier, as far back as 1567. In that usage, “ends” meant leftover pieces, while “odd” meant something extra or out of the ordinary.English has plenty of other expressions for assorted odds and ends, including the British phrases "bits and bobs," "bits and bats," "odds and sods," and "odds and bobs."Another similar phrase, "bits and pieces," may not be quite as interchangeable with "odds and ends" as it seems. "Bits and pieces" can refer to literal fragments of something broken or taken apart, but they can also describe doing something little by little. Sometimes, they simply mean the miscellaneous things you pick up along the way.There’s also a word for those random leftovers and stray items you may not be familiar with: oddment. This noun can refer to a remnant or miscellaneous article. It might be useful when describing the contents of a cluttered shelf, a junk drawer, or, after Thanksgiving, the refrigerator.To hear more about the words we use for life's leftovers, listen to the audio above.

articles.description: Mexico's government is slamming a DEA crime tip line as foreign interference. Others are thrilled. AP News Mexico files formal complaint to US over DEA tip line ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum protests new DEA tip line for reporting criminals, corrupt officials Fox News Mexico condemns DEA tip line asking people to report corrupt officials in Sinaloa The Washington
articles.content: MEXICO CITY (AP) — The government in Mexico is railing against the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency’s anonymous tip line for reports against criminals and corrupt officials in the Latin American nation, slamming it as foreign interference. In the state of Sinaloa, journalist Juan Manuel Partida Valdez was among the first to write to the WhatsApp line on Thursday, just a day after DEA chief Terry Cole called for anonymous reports on his X account. The announcement opened the latest chapter in an ongoing struggle between the U.S. and Mexican governments over who has the right to take action against cartels in Mexico. Partida Valdez, president of the Sinaloa Journalists Association, said he sent information about alleged ties between Sinaloa politicians and criminal groups because authorities have failed to put an end to violence and corruption that has bled his northern Mexican region dry in recent years. “I talk to so many people — in the streets, on social media, on WhatsApp and in chats — and you realize what people think: We’re all fed up,” the 67-year-old told The Associated Press on Friday. “We’re fed up with narco-governments.” On Friday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said she escalated her fight with Washington over the tip line, filing a formal complaint with the U.S. Embassy for interfering in Mexico’s internal affairs. “We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination,” Sheinbaum said in her morning press briefing. Sheinbaum once again urged Washington to address drug use and combat drug traffickers within its own territory while affirming that Mexico would continue working to confront cartels and prevent drugs from reaching the U.S. As U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Sheinbaum to crack down on criminal groups, Sheinbaum has underscored Mexican sovereignty at the same time her government has cracked down on cartels more forcefully than her predecessors. Homicide rates have taken a sharp dip in Mexico and the government has taken out a number of top cartel bosses, often using U.S. intelligence to do so. The latest came over the weekend, when Mexican forces captured an important ally of a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, and requested that a U.S. surveillance drone fly over Mexican territory to help them pinpoint the location of the capo. At the same time, a number of scandals have soured that relationship. In April, two CIA agents died following a drug lab bust with local authorities in northern Chihuahua. Sheinbaum said her government was not informed that two U.S. intelligence agents were carrying out an operation in Mexican territory, paving the way for a potential treason trial. Weeks later, Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya — a powerful figure in Sheinbaum’s party — was forced to step down after he was indicted by the U.S. on drug-trafficking charges in another political blow. It was this case that Partida Valdez, the journalist, cited as a key reason for why he decided to reach out to the tip line, saying it was a “very clear example of what we’re suffering because of these governments that do absolutely nothing but protect criminals.” “This whole song and dance about sovereignty is just collusion with the politicians tied to drug trafficking who are being protected in our country,” he added. While a number of observers warned of the dangers of the strategy by the DEA, other academics and politicians celebrated the line as a potential tool or said they trusted the intelligence agency more than their own government. Lilly Téllez, a senator for Mexico’s National Action Party, a weakened opposition party that has also been plagued by a number of corruption scandals, said she welcomed the tip line. Téllez, a politician from the U.S.-Mexico border state of Sonora, wrote on X on Friday that the tip line is “a good way to cooperate against the common enemy of both countries” and strengthens efforts to combat cartels. “On behalf of millions of Mexicans oppressed by the cartels, I ask President (Sheinbaum) not to obstruct the opportunity to gather more information to locate criminals and identify their activities,” she wrote. ___ Associated Press journalist Megan Janetsky contributed to this report from Mexico City.

articles.title: Little Free Libraries provide books, community sharing
articles.description: By NAOMI MAXWELL Capital News Service Michigan has community-run book exchanges called Little Free Libraries, located in neighborhoods, parks, schools and outside local organizations. The boxes, often mounted on poles, […]
articles.content: By NAOMI MAXWELL Capital News Service Michigan has community-run book exchanges called Little Free Libraries, located in neighborhoods, parks, schools and outside local organizations. The boxes, often mounted on poles, let community members leave a book for others to enjoy or pick up a new book for free. Michigan now has more than 3,400 such book exchanges across the state after seeing steady increases over the last decade, according to the Little Free Libraries website. The Towar of Flowers Book Nook, a Little Free Library in East Lansing. Photo by Naomi Maxwell That does not include the little libraries that people build independently from the organization, so it’s likely there are more across the state. According to the Little Free Libraries website, its Impact Library Program “provides no-cost Little Free Library book-sharing boxes to underserved communities where they can make a meaningful impact on book access and literacy engagement.” The website has a map where people can find libraries in their area by searching with their zip code. In Ann Arbor, a Little Free Library is located on the grounds of Leslie Science and Nature Center. Susan Westhoff, CEO of the science center, said, “We have over 50,000 people on our site every year. Many are children, and the idea of providing a space for books to be exchanged or found was very appealing.” The Little Free Library box has been around for quite a few years, but Westhoff said it has become more popular recently. “I’ve seen more changeover in the books since mid-summer, which made me so happy.” In the first few years, staff brought books in to keep the library going, Westhoff said. Additionally, she said, “We know we have kids coming by that have books at home, but from some of our conversations there are children who do not have that luxury.” Her hope is that when children visit the center, “they may find a new treasure to take home with them.” As far as restocking the library, “We encourage the public to restock, and in the summer we message our camp families to encourage its use. We have about 900 campers on site during the summer, so it’s a great opportunity to use the Little Free Library for something new to read,” Westhoff said. Kids have many interests, from graphic novels to classics. For example, a current beloved series is “Dog Man,” according to Westhoff. Parents also enjoy little libraries, from fiction to nonfiction, she said. In Howell, a chapter of the Little Free Libraries program is called Reading in the Ravines. Another Little Free Library, the Towar of Flowers Book Nook in East Lansing’s Towar Gardens neighborhood, won one of the city’s Crystal Awards. The award recognizes organizations, businesses and individuals that support the community. A local public library in Big Rapids emphasized the importance of free libraries. According to its website, “These tiny libraries serve as gathering places, bringing neighbors together and facilitating meaningful conversations. They symbolize generosity and collective action, demonstrating knowledge and making it accessible to all.” As the boxes remind users, “Take a book, leave a book.” Help free little libraries this weekend This weekend, shoppers around the nation will take part in Small Business Saturday, a community-focused counterpart to Black Friday and Cyber Monday. In celebration, a local organization is encouraging community members to donate books at area small businesses. The organization, called Makenna’s Books, was founded in honor of Makenna Morse, an Eaton Rapids English teacher who died in a car crash in 2024. Makenna’s Books collects donations and distributes them to Little Free Libraries across the state in memory of Morse and other literary enthusiasts who have passed. Nearly 3,000 books have been donated so far. Donors can drop off books at the following businesses from Friday (Nov. 27) through Monday (Nov. 30): Barrett’s Books, 111 W. Grand River Ave., Williamston Bestsellers Books & Coffee, 360 S. Jefferson St., Mason Sis’s Stories, 617 E. Saginaw Hwy., Grand Ledge The Cozy Corner Bookstore, 144 S. Cochran Ave., Charlotte Darrell’s Market & Hardware, 4520 W. Columbia Road, Mason Participants will be entered into a drawing for a $25 gift card to the store they made their donation at. Books are labeled with the name of the donor and the loved one they’re honoring. For more information, visit makennasbooks.com.

articles.title: Mamdani quietly handed staffers nearly $1M in raises — even on same day he warned of ‘massive’ budget deficit
articles.content: See more of our coverage in your search results. Mayor Zohran Mamdani doled out nearly $1 million in pay raises to dozens of City Hall staffers since taking office — even handing out pay bumps on the same day he claimed to be checking “every single dollar” in the Big Apple’s budget. The democratic socialist mayor — who recited a “tax the rich” rallying cry throughout his campaign last year — doled out raises worth a collective $850,000 since January to at least 46 staffers, according to a Post review of city records. That sum included 21 first-time hires who were rewarded with $450,000 in raises before they had even reached a year on the job, the records show. It’s more than twice the number of first-timers who got raises under both mayors Eric Adams and Bill de Blasio. Critics were left shaking their heads over the move, especially since Mamdani vowed to open a period “defined by transparency” when he won Gracie Mansion in 2025. “You got hired and accepted a salary and less than a year later — you got a pay raise?” veteran Democratic strategist Bill Cunningham asked. “That’s not sending a good signal to the taxpayers that you’re serious about dealing with any of these ongoing budget challenges.” Five City Hall staffers were even awarded a collective $95,000 in raises on Jan. 28 — the same day Mamdani announced the Big Apple was facing a budget deficit his office claimed to be about $12 billion. “There is a massive fiscal deficit in our city’s budget to the tune of at least $12 billion,” he claimed at the time. Hizzoner said his team was “looking at every single dollar that the city spends.” That deficit was later reassessed to about $5.4 billion. But it didn’t stop Mamdani from proclaiming a crisis of “historic magnitude” — then using it to pressure Gov. Kathy Hochul into passing his “tax the rich” agenda, threatening to impose a 9.5% residential property tax on New Yorkers to close the gap if Albany didn’t give in. Hochul, a Democrat then facing re-election, eventually took the bait and helped Mamdani push through his controversial pied-à-terre tax on second homes in the city over the summer. The extra cash helped him finalize a budget he said “scoured for savings.” There was apparently plenty of cash for raises, however, with some staffers seeing their salaries increasing by 50% or more. Those raises included: Mamdani himself has rebuffed collecting any increases of his roughly $260,000 salary, but the staff raises were still a far cry from what other New York leaders have done in the past. Cunningham, a onetime aide to both former Gov. Mario Cuomo and ex-Mayor Mike Bloomberg, noted Cuomo made a point of freezing all raises when the state faced a budget crisis. The Presidential Administration and UNICEF Celebrate 80 Years of Global Impact for Children and 35 Years of Progress in Romania
articles.content: BUCHAREST, 26 November 2026 - The Presidential Administration and UNICEF celebrated on Thursday, at the Cotroceni Palace, two significant milestones: 80 years of achievements by UNICEF for children around the world and 35 years of partnership and progress in Romania. The anniversary event took place under the High Patronage of the President of Romania and brought together senior government officials, members of Parliament, representatives of the diplomatic corps, civil society and the private sector, children and young people, journalists, as well as numerous advocates for children’s rights. Over the past eight decades, UNICEF and its partners have helped drive some of the world's most significant advances for children, contributing to dramatic reductions in child mortality, expanding access to immunization and education, and improving children's health, nutrition, protection and well-being worldwide. In Romania, UNICEF has worked alongside national and local authorities, communities, professionals and families since 1991. During the three and a half decades of cooperation between UNICEF and Romania, significant progress for children was achieved. Among the key achievements to which UNICEF has contributed are reforms in the field of child protection, the expansion of access to high-quality inclusive education and health services, the development of integrated community-based services, children’s participation in decision-making, and the support provided to refugee children and their families. “Behind UNICEF’s history lie millions of stories of life, hope and courage,” said Mirabela Grădinaru, First Lady of Romania. “On this anniversary, the best tribute we can pay to all those who have contributed over the years to improving children’s lives is to renew our own commitment to each and every one of them. Let us build a Romania in which no child feels alone, forgotten or deprived of opportunities. A Romania in which every child can grow up with confidence, joy and hope for a better future, because every child deserves a happy childhood, and the way we look after today’s children says, perhaps more than anything else, what sort of society we want to be tomorrow,” she added. "Today we celebrate remarkable results for children and we renew the commitment to ensuring that every child can survive, thrive and fulfil their potential," said Anna Riatti, UNICEF Representative to Romania. "The story of UNICEF's first 80 years shows that when governments, political leaders, communities, international partners, businesses and young people come together, change happens, lives are saved, opportunities are created and the future is transformed. As UNICEF enters its ninth decade globally and continues its work in Romania, we reaffirm our commitment to for the future of every child." The anniversary programme included a reception attended by guests and partners, as well as a special musical performance by the Cantus Mundi National Programme, celebrating the power of children and young people to inspire hope, solidarity and positive change. UNICEF promotes the rights and wellbeing of every child, in everything we do. Together with our partners, we work in 190 countries and territories to translate that commitment into practical action, focusing special effort on reaching the most vulnerable and excluded children, to the benefit of all children, everywhere. For more information about UNICEF and its work for children, visit www.unicef.org.

Historic low in measles deaths, but immunization gaps threaten progress
articles.content: Worldwide measles deaths are at a historic low as more children are vaccinated, the World Health Organization (WHO) said in a report released today. In 2025, an estimated 72 000 people died from measles worldwide, a 91% reduction since 2000. However, vaccination coverage remains insufficient and uneven across many countries, putting progress towards measles elimination at risk. Looking at global measles over the past 25 years, the report estimates that measles vaccination has saved more than 60 million lives since 2000. “Measles deaths have never been lower, thanks to the extraordinary life-saving power of vaccines," said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. "But measles does not forgive complacency. Countries that had eliminated it are now losing that status. Elimination is not a finish line. It must be defended, with two doses of vaccine for every child, everywhere." Globally, nearly 10 million people were estimated to have been infected with measles in 2025. While this is among the lowest estimated levels reported, trends varied substantially by region. In the Region of the Americas, case numbers increased 8-fold since 2000, with 73 000 people infected in 2025. Nearly half of the global cases occurred in the South-East Asia Region. While global measles immunization coverage remained largely unchanged in 2025, with 84% of children receiving a first dose and 77% receiving a second dose, the global trends mask regional and national declines and inequities. The Region of the Americas has seen immunization coverage decline from levels above 90% before the COVID-19 pandemic. Most concerning is the recent loss of measles elimination status in several countries. Several countries in the European Region also recorded some of the lowest measles immunization coverage rates despite the overall regional coverage rate for the first dose remaining high at 92%. There are stark inequalities in access to immunization. Low-income countries reported coverage of just 69% for the first dose and 57% for the second, compared with 93% and 91%, respectively, in high-income countries. Children in conflict and crisis settings also remain far less likely to be vaccinated and bear a disproportionate burden of measles outbreaks. More than 29 million children were unvaccinated or under-immunized against measles in 2025, making them vulnerable to the disease. That year, 59 countries experienced large or disruptive measles outbreaks, including 18 low-income countries, 34 middle-income countries, and seven high-income countries. Eleven outbreaks occurred in countries that had previously been declared measles-free. Even in places with better access to nutrition and health care, children infected with measles can still develop severe, lifelong complications, such as blindness, pneumonia, and encephalitis, which can cause brain damage and lead to death. By the end of 2025, 95 countries had been verified as having achieved or maintained measles elimination. However, ongoing challenges, including the recent loss of elimination status in several countries underscore that elimination is not the finish line. Without consistently high vaccination coverage in every community, strong surveillance systems and sustained political will, the virus can quickly regain a foothold. Ending measles outbreaks means reaching every child, everywhere. The Measles & Rubella Partnership is working with governments worldwide to strengthen political commitment to measles elimination; invest in stronger surveillance and routine immunization systems; enhance outbreak response, including through the M&RP Outbreak Response Fund; and build community trust in measles vaccination. Dedicated to the well-being of all people and guided by science, WHO leads and champions global efforts to give everyone, everywhere, an equal chance at a safe and healthy life. We are the United Nations’ agency for health that connects nations, partners and people in more than 150 locations – leading the world’s response to health emergencies, preventing disease, addressing the root causes of health issues and expanding access to medicines and health care. Our mission is to support all countries to promote, provide and protect health. “Together for health. Stand with science”, the theme of World Health Day 2026, marks a year-long campaign to highlight science as the foundation for protecting health and well-being worldwide. The Measles & Rubella Partnership (M&RP) is a global initiative to lead and coordinate efforts to achieve a world without measles and rubella. M&RP is led by the American Red Cross, the Gates Foundation, Gavi the Vaccine Alliance, the United Nations Foundation, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, UNICEF and the World Health Organization.

911 emergency? Michigan counties turning to voters to keep services running
articles.description: Several Michigan counties renewed or increased 911 surcharges this year, one of the funding options available for emergency services. Depending on where you live, that could mean a higher phone bill, but advocates say it’s worth having a fully-funded 911 system.
articles.content: Voters in several Michigan counties voted this year to increase or renew local monthly phone surcharges to cover 911 costs Dispatchers in counties that requested the fees say they play an important role in keeping emergency services operational Most recent surcharge requests have passed, but voters in one county rejected an increase and officials in another have concerns Amid technology updates and increasing costs of answering 911 calls, more Michigan counties are turning to voters to boost local funds for emergency services. On Nov. 3, voters in Jackson, Grand Traverse, Alcona and Presque Isle counties approved increases to or renewals of local 911 surcharge fees that appear on residents’ phone bills each month. Earlier this year, voters in Alpena, Hillsdale and Shiawassee counties also approved surcharge increases or renewals, while voters in Oscoda County rejected a similar measure. First responders say 911 surcharges are a critical funding source for emergency services, especially in communities where the localized fees are the primary source of funding keeping the 911 system up and running. “If something breaks, we’ve got to be able to have the money available,” said Corey LeCureux, director of Grand Traverse County 911 / Central Dispatch, noting that fixing anything awry in a 911 center “costs hundreds of thousands of dollars, and it’s usually a critical program that we need to get online yesterday.” Related: Most Michigan school bonds pass in Nov. election. Look up your district Here’s how Michigan voted on school millages, other tax increase proposals Benzie County operations in doubt after voters defeat tax to pay bills “The pitch that we gave to the voters was, we’re doing well, but we need to be continuing to do well into the future,” added LeCureux, whose county approved a 50-cent increase from $2.50 to a $3 surcharge. Why surcharges? More than 80% of counties in Michigan have some form of local surcharge for 911 services, though how much is tacked onto each individual phone line varies widely by county, according to data compiled by the Michigan Public Service Commission and Michigan’s State 911 Committee. That’s in addition to a statewide 25-cent fee, most of which is split between counties quarterly through both a flat payment and per-capita distribution, and recurring technical charges. County commissions can approve 911 monthly per-line surcharges of up to $0.42, but voter-approval is needed for higher surcharges, which are currently capped at $3. With the latest voter-approved changes, more than 40% of counties will charge at least $2.00 a month for the services once the new fees take effect next summer. Donate Because there’s no single statewide funding system for 911 services, many local governments pay for their emergency dispatch using a mix of surcharges, local property taxes or general funds. Others rely almost exclusively on surcharge revenue. How are the funds used? Under state law, funding from local 911 surcharges can only be used on staffing, facilities, technology or training related directly to 911 response. That can range from the daily operating costs of keeping 911 dispatch centers staffed and prepared for emergencies to larger technology investments. In Jackson County, voters agreed to double their monthly surcharge from $1.50 to the $3.00 maximum to help the county purchase new emergency radios for first responders. Jason Hamman, the emergency dispatch 911 director for Jackson County Central Dispatch, said a countywide surcharge can be an easier sell for voters than a local tax increase, in part because it’s a fairer split — regardless of whether someone owns property or not, they have equal buy-in on a service that benefits the entire community. The radios required for the county’s emergency operations cost between $7,000 and $9,000 apiece, Hamman added. If it were left up to local municipalities to come up with that money, either through shifting budgets or putting up a millage request, “those townships might not have radios…and that’s not good when there’s an emergency going on,” he said. For Alpena County Central Dispatch, daily operations and employee wages are “100% funded by our surcharge,” Director Kim Elkie said. Anything else, whether a recent technology integration with local fire and EMS or the department’s participation in the city’s annual Trunk or Treat event, must be paid for through a request to the county or out of employees’ own pockets. The funds “come with a lot of strings, and we live and die on that hill,” she said. “We sleep very soundly at night, knowing that we have appropriately spent our funds.” Much of the surcharge money goes to making sure the county is prepared for when residents need 911 most, including having backup systems ready during major outages, Elkie said. The county dispatch maintains four layers of capabilities to answer calls, she said — during a major ice storm that hit the region in 2025, “we operated on our third level of equipment.” “That technology is a huge part of our costs, providing those layers of redundancy,” she said. Too much, not enough or just right? In Grand Traverse County, the boost in surcharge fees was largely an acknowledgement of the rapidly rising costs of 911 technology, LeCureux said. “This will give us a little bit of breathing room,” he said of the surcharge increase. “We felt like it was the responsible thing to do for public safety.” Looking ahead, however, he and other dispatchers in counties at or near the maximum surcharge limit fear the $3-per-phone line surcharge won’t always be enough to maintain current operations while keeping up with technology upgrades. For rural areas already relying on the surcharges, a slightly higher maximum cap would give dispatchers “room to gradually bake in some additional raises that won’t hurt so much,” LeCureux said. To do that, state lawmakers and the governor would need to agree to change state law. “I think that’s something that the voters would be open to,” LeCureux continued. “We can’t just lift the cap altogether, I get that, but we can make it a little bit more relevant for our current situation in 2026.” In other regions of the state with minimal surcharges, first responders see the fee as an opportunity to bring in more funding to improve 911 response, though voters and local officials haven’t always been on board. A majority of Oscoda County voters determined a jump from $0.45 per line to $3.00 per line was too much, too fast, with 55% voting to reject the proposal. And in Washtenaw County, county commissioners rejected a request by County Sheriff Alyshia Dyer to put a surcharge increase before voters on the November ballot. The county currently has a $0.43 local surcharge, with much of the system’s other funding needs covered by contracts with local agencies and general fund dollars. Several commissioners said at the time that they still had unanswered questions about how the additional surcharge would benefit residents. But in a July interview with Bridge Michigan, Dyer was optimistic that leveraging the fee could be a step toward improving response to mental health calls. As Bridge reported in February, the county has grappled with how best to respond to mental health crises in Michigan after a multi-day standoff between a Ypsilanti man and a SWAT team sparked community outcry. “911 is critical — you need it to work,” she previously told Bridge. “Making it better and improving response times, as well as putting social workers in dispatch and saving local municipalities and the county funding, I think, is a win-win for a lot of people, but it’s a win for public safety.”

Secret donors helped Democratic nominees dominate Michigan Supreme Court races
articles.description: Dark money groups spent more than $2 million to help Michigan Supreme Court justices nominated by the Democratic Party retain a 6-1 advantage on the state’s highest court.
articles.content: Democrat-nominated Supreme Court candidates received more than $2 million in disclosed outside help. GOP nominees almost nothing. Six of Michigan’s seven supreme court justices have been nominated by Democrats, as Republicans have been repeatedly outspent. Justices Megan Cavanagh and Noah Hood will serve new seven-year terms after getting more than twice the votes of GOP opponents LANSING — More than $2 million in dark money spending helped Democrat-nominated Michigan Supreme Court justices win reelection and maintain a six-to-one majority on the state’s highest court, according to the most recently available campaign finance reports. Justices Megan Cavanagh and Noah Hood — who as incumbents both appeared on the ballot with the potent “Justice of the Supreme Court” label — each received more than double the votes of their Republican challengers. They both won by larger percentages than other leading Democratic candidates on the ballot, including Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson. Beyond the incumbency label, Cavanagh and Hood also had some help in the form of millions of dollars in spending from outside organizations that don’t have to disclose their donors, continuing a trend of dominant Democratic victories fueled by significant fundraising advantages. Outside groups reported spending nearly $2.5 million to boost the Democratic nominees through mid-October. Republican nominees Michael Warren and Casandra Morse-Bills, on the other hand, had received just $3,100 in disclosed outside spending to assist them. Related: Incumbents reelected to Michigan Supreme Court ‘Dark money’ helped Dems dominate 2024 Michigan Supreme Court races Progressives grow sway in Lansing, push to tax the rich and corporations The final totals are likely higher, as committees have yet to disclose the extent of their fundraising and spending through the election. Post-election filings are due in early December. While dark money spending has proliferated in political races across the country, experts have called it a particularly worrisome trend in judicial races, where candidates may later be tasked with deciding cases involving persons or companies that secretly funded their election. “This flood of secret money leaves voters without important information about the interests trying to shape state courts, and it can obscure potential conflicts of interest for judges and litigants alike,” Alicia Bannon of the nonpartisan Brennan Center for Justice wrote in a 2018 report. The Michigan Supreme Court often has the final say on issues of critical importance, including whether laws enacted by the state Legislature are constitutional or whether ballot measures should go before voters. Donate The court has in recent months made several precedent-setting decisions on criminal law, including limits on the constitutionality of mandatory life without parole sentences and a ruling declaring the state’s sex offender registry law unconstitutional if applied retroactively. The latter decision has already resulted in the removal of more than 20,000 people from the list. The court also adopted a rule this year aiming to limit the ability of law enforcement officers to make civil arrests — including immigration arrests of suspected noncitizens — in state and local courtrooms. One outside group, the Justice For All super PAC, has spent more than $15 million since 2020 supporting Democratic nominees running for the state’s highest court. The PAC is linked to the Michigan Association for Justice, which represents trial lawyers. For 2026, two dark money nonprofits made up the vast majority of the super PAC’s fundraising through mid-October: The Michigan Civic Action Fund gave $1.75 million, while Justice Project Action provided $1.38 million. The Michigan Civic Action Fund won’t have to disclose its 2026 spending until November 2027, but in 2024, the most recent available year, the organization reported taking in $14.6 million and spending $15.6 million. A representative for the fund, Amy Chapman, didn’t respond to a request for comment on this story. Justice Project Action, meanwhile, is a national group that has also been involved in the expensive judicial elections in other states. Beyond those two dark money groups, billionaire Democrat Michael Bloomberg also gave $375,000 to the Justice For All super PAC, according to the latest campaign finance reports. He gave $1 million to support Democratic nominees in the state’s 2024 Supreme Court election. Three labor unions, the Michigan Laborers District Council, Michigan regional council of Carpenters and United Auto Workers also donated a combined $210,000 to Justice For All. Michigan Supreme Court races are far down the ballot, and though candidates are nominated by political parties, the contests are technically nonpartisan. As a result, judicial hopefuls typically see far fewer votes than other candidates, as straight-ticket voters who don’t complete their ballots end up leaving those races blank. But “liberals and folks on the left have focused on making sure that people know how to vote their entire ballot,” said liberal consultant Lonnie Scott. “That’s ballot measures. It’s school board races. It’s lots of things beyond the Supreme Court.” Spending related to judicial races can also go undisclosed for other reasons. Nonprofits can send advertisements urging voters to complete their entire ballot without triggering disclosure requirements under Michigan’s campaign finance law. There are nuanced federal tax rules about who can be targeted by those mailings and ads — it can’t be an explicitly political list — but it allows their proponents to spend in ways that others cannot.

articles.title: WHO issues updated Ebola response recommendations, calling for improved security and accelerated research
articles.content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has updated its recommendations for the Ebola epidemic caused by the Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), following a meeting of the Emergency Committee convened by the WHO Director-General under the International Health Regulations (2005). The Committee called for faster clinical trials of candidate vaccines and treatments while maintaining high scientific, ethical and safety standards. Engaging communities was identified as key for the promotion of clear and transparent information on how the trials are planned and implemented. Over 12 000 cases of Ebola and 5900 deaths had been reported in the DRC as of 24 November. Insecurity remains a significant obstacle to efforts to contain the outbreak, with direct repercussions on humanitarian access and the protection of patients, health workers, responders, and health facilities. WHO has verified at least 94 attacks on health care in the DRC since the outbreak was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) six months ago. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus issued the updated recommendations on 25 November 2026 after concurring with the advice of the third meeting of the Emergency Committee on 17 November. The Director-General also determined that the epidemic continues to constitute a PHEIC. “Six months into this emergency, the Committee remains deeply concerned by continued transmission and the high number of Ebola-related deaths, particularly in a context where insecurity and obstacles to reaching affected communities make every aspect of the response more difficult,” said Professor Lucille Blumberg, Chair of the Emergency Committee. “Stopping Ebola will require coordinated and accelerated action to find cases earlier, prevent infections in health-care settings and in the community, provide early supportive care, maintain trust with communities, and ensure responders can safely reach people in need.” The Committee emphasized the need to prevent transmission in health facilities, including infections associated with unsafe injection practices, and to reduce delays between the onset of symptoms, diagnosis and access to supportive care. The updated recommendations call for intensified action in areas of the DRC where new BVD cases are occurring or community transmission is increasing. For other countries, WHO recommends targeted measures to identify and assess travelers who may have been exposed to BVD to reduce the risk of spread beyond the DRC. These recommendations aim to stop transmission at its source and protect affected communities and health workers, without unnecessarily interfering with flights and international traffic. An Emergency Committee, under the provisions of the IHR, is a group of experts convened by the WHO Director-General to provide advice on whether a public health event constitutes, or may constitute, a PHEIC. The Committee also advises on temporary recommendations to countries, as proposed by the WHO Secretariat, which the WHO Director-General shall issue in the context of PHEICs. Members of an Emergency Committee are selected by the WHO Director-General from a pool of experts. Since the International Health Regulations (2005) entered into force in 2007, the WHO Director-General has convened Emergency Committees in relation to 12 public health events, nine of which were determined to constitute PHEICs – including outbreaks of Ebola, Zika, mpox and COVID-19. articles.title: Two Macomb County families grow with adoptions
articles.content: Two Macomb County families formally welcomed new additions to their families last Tuesday in the annual Michigan Adoption Day, the only time adoptions are publicly granted. Macomb Circuit Court Juvenile Judge Joseph Toia OK’s the adoptions following brief hearings in the Mount Clemens courthouse. The cases had already been thoroughly reviewed by adoption officials. Annette Henton of Clinton Township adopted her grandson, Syaire, 10, after foster caring for him the past four years. Syaire’s biological mother is Henton’s daughter-in-law. “Rather than see my baby in the system, he’s with grandma Henton, so he’s always with family,” Henton said. “He spends a lot of time with his maternal grandparents because they have his older brother. I wanted to keep the family close. If he was going to be in the system, he was going to be with me.” Family members attended in support of the move, includiung Syaire’s aunts Donna Willis and Etta Henton, and Annette Henton’s son, Tadario Henton. Syaire attends Mark Twain Elementary School in Fraser. Now that he’s formally Henton’s son, “We decided I am still going to be ‘grandma,’” Henton said. Syaire, who dressed in his favorite color, red, was categorized as a relative adoption though the Michigan Adoption Resource Exchange, (MARE). Meanwhile, Joseph Palmer and Patrick Walter of Shelby Township adopted 9-month-old Zoey Lynn Palmer, who has been with them since shortly after birth, through an agency, Adoption Partners of Michigan. “They didn’t hesitate to say yes to her adoption in early March when they got the call about a baby who had been surrendered under the Safe Delivery of Newborns law,” said Michelle Dykema of Adoption Partners of Michigan. “They have cared for her as their own. “She’s grown to become a feisty, opinionated, strong but incredibly adorable little girl who fits right in. She will no doubt continue to thrive and grow in their care.” Dykema added that in her experience at her organization “we see it all the time, just how babies find their to just the right family, just the right home. It’s amazing to witness.” Walter said he “always wanted a few kids.” “I always grew up with a family and always thought of myself as wanting the safe tradition, sharing the same things with my kids,” Walter said. Palmer and Walter previously adopted Evan, who is 8. Also at the event, four agencies operated information display tables – Macomb Foster Closet in Mount Clemens, Friends of Foster Kids in Utica, MARE and Post Adoption Resource Centers in Southfield. Dozens of Adoption Day ceremonies were held at courthouses across the state. Michigan courts have participated in Adoption Day celebrations for 24 years to bring attention to the importance of adoption and the need for permanent homes for children in foster care. “Celebrating new families on Adoption Day is my favorite way to begin the holiday season,” said Amy Epkey, acting director of the state Department of Health and Human services. “It’s a joy to celebrate children finding the security, love and stability of a forever family and to honor the people who have opened their hearts and homes through adoption.” “Michigan Adoption Day serves as a reminder that adoption is more than a legal proceeding,” state court officials said. “It represents the beginning of a new chapter for children and families and the enduring importance of belonging, stability, and lifelong connections.” In Michigan, there are about 10,000 children in foster care and 1,700 children in the adoption process, including about 190 children who are waiting to be matched with an adoptive family, according to DHHS. In fiscal year 2026, MDHHS, along with contracted private adoption agency partners, helped secure “forever homes” for 1,122 children, officials said. To learn more about adoption, go to michigan.gov/mdhhs/adult-child-serv/adoption. To learn more about MARE, visit mare.org/. Deadlocked final result in New Zealand’s election leaves a centrist newcomer as the decider
articles.description: Deadlocked final result in New Zealand’s election leaves a centrist newcomer as the decider AP News Final New Zealand election vote count to confirm parliament make up Reuters Could New Zealand head back to the polls? The new centrist party on the block holds the power| Lara Greaves The Guardian Political novice turns kingmaker after New Zealand’s deadlocked election The Washington Post New Zealand election results s
articles.content: WELLINGTON, New Zealand (AP) — The final vote count in New Zealand’s election published Friday showed neither the right-wing incumbents nor the left-wing opposition bloc won enough seats to form a majority, giving a centrist party new to Parliament the balance of power in deciding the shape of the next government. It left conservative Prime Minister Christopher Luxon the only leader with a viable path to victory, but he faces the prospect of fraught negotiations with three divergent minor parties who will seek deep policy concessions to secure their support. Endorsement from all three would be necessary to break the election deadlock and return Luxon’s center-right National party for a second term in office. The election on Nov. 7 was the tightest vote in years, and the conservative bloc finished the night with a wafer-thin majority. But after counting 400,000 so-called special votes, including those cast by New Zealanders living abroad, the Electoral Commission said Friday that National had lost two seats, finishing with 40. The right-wing parties now have a collective 65 seats in a 130-seat parliament, one short of the 66 needed for a majority government. The left-wing opposition, led by the Labour party’s Chris Hipkins, won 58 seats, up by one from election night. Labour itself won 36 of those seats. The figures leave a new entrant to Parliament, the Opportunity party — an unaligned centrist group that won seven seats — with the ultimate power to propel Luxon to power. Opportunity’s support wouldn’t be enough to install a left-wing government, Hipkins admitted on Friday in an apparent concession of defeat. Luxon said Friday that he was confident he could form a government with Opportunity and his traditional partners, the libertarian ACT and the populist NZ First. However, his route to power is not simple because some of Opportunity’s socially liberal, technocratic and pro-environment values are at odds with the policies of parties on the right. Opportunity is led by 38-year-old business consultant and political newcomer Qiulae Wong, who has said she could work with either side to form a government. Wong’s pledges of evidence-based centrism and an end to partisan bickering apparently appealed to voters, who delivered a stinging rebuke to the major parties that have long dominated New Zealand politics. The final count showed more support for minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. A total of 2.8 million votes were cast. Among the right-wing parties that have traditionally supported National, ACT won 13 seats and NZ First won 12. Out of the parties supporting Labour, the left-leaning Greens won 17 seats and Te Pati Māori, an Indigenous rights group, won five. New Zealanders cast two votes in elections, one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative. The country has only one house of parliament, and no states, which means that the central government has ultimate sway over the country’s direction. Both Labour and National secured less than 30% of the preferred party vote. Analysts said it reflected voters’ malaise about high living costs and a lack of enthusiasm for both Luxon, who survived two confidence votes among his lawmakers this year, and Hipkins, who led Labour to a 2023 election loss. At the final count, National won 28.35% and Labour 29.88%. National, however, secured more seats in Parliament because more of its candidates won local races. Luxon vehemently ruled out working with Opportunity before the election, a position he reversed on Friday when Wong’s support became the only way to form a government. If a government can’t be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh vote. Elections in New Zealand are typically held every three years. Making a deal will be a grueling task. Opportunity’s five so-called “bottom line” policies include stronger measures on climate change and an end to bottom-trawling fisheries, which are in direct opposition to the stances of NZ First and ACT. Wong also repeated Friday a position that she would not enter a government where NZ First leader Winston Peters served as Foreign Minister, a role he held until the election. Peters has been lambasted by his detractors for remarks he has made in Parliament about Asian people, which Wong said made him unsuitable to represent New Zealand abroad. On Friday, Luxon didn’t divulge how he might solve those conflicts. But he warned that the country could face a long wait for a government. “These negotiations may be challenging and they could take some time,” he said. “But getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly.” Wong told reporters that her party would consider a formal coalition deal or a so-called “confidence and supply” agreement, in which Opportunity’s lawmakers would agree to back key government legislation and support other bills on a case by case basis. Opportunity’s kingmaker role was a staggering ascension for a party that made three failed attempts at Parliament before Wong became leader less than a year ago. None of its incoming members have been lawmakers before.

Michigan woman took aging mother’s care into her own hands. She’s not alone
articles.description: As an aging population puts demand on a health care system that outstrips supply, many families have to make tough choices about caring for their loved ones.
articles.content: A new report found the home health aid industry struggles to recruit and retain employees, forcing many family members to become unpaid caregivers The aging baby boomer population is straining the healthcare industry, creating demand that outstrips supply, raising prices One woman took matters into her own hands, using her human resources experience to hire a nurse for her aging mother From keeping things tidy and scheduling a host of medical appointments to spending hours sorting insurance claims and transferring a loved one from the bed to the car, caring for a sick spouse or aging family member can be a tall order. Alternatively, affording a paid caregiver, assisted care facility or nursing home has become an even taller order for the average U.S. household. Between 2019 to 2024, the cost for homemaker, home health and assisted living services increased by 46% to 48%, or an annual average rate of increase of 8%, according to AARP. Adult day services and nursing homes also increased at a faster rate than income. Theresa de la Osa of Troy, Michigan, felt that increase overnight — twice. In 2025, her mother required intensive in-home care following a fall and soon after needed to move to an assisted living facility. De la Osa said half of the money spent on her mother’s in-home care went directly into the pockets of an Oakland County company instead of the nurses. Later, the daily rate for the Macomb County facility where her mother lived more than quadrupled — from $19 to $85. There was no way she or her mother could sustain such increases. Having just started a business that same year as an executive recruiter, de la Osa ultimately used her human resource talent acquisition skills to find in-home care for her mother at a more affordable rate. RELATED: Michigan’s aging fast, but many seniors unaware of services, poll finds As Michigan ages, are we overlooking a critical type of caregiver – the friend? Michigan sits on $35M fund to improve nursing homes. It’s largely unused “We had hired a company where a few women came in to provide care for my mother,” said de la Osa, an executive recruiter with an international software company based in Seattle, Washington. “I realized some of these women were getting $15 to $16 an hour, but we were paying the company $33 an hour. I got to talking to a physical therapist that I know and he said, ‘You know, you may want to reach out to nursing schools to find someone directly.’” She added that the company-provided care partners were actually not medically trained, thus inexperienced in making emergency judgement calls and unable to administer medication. This put a lot of responsibility back on de la Osa while still taking a big financial toll. Taking matters into her own hands De la Osa, 52, immediately decided to become the care recruiter her mother needed to ensure an affordable and attentive care experience. Donate “I began using my recruiting skills, finding somebody that had a nursing background,” she said. “I’m really into AI, so I used Claude and Chat GPT — simple as that — to find out what the local nursing schools were. Many of them have some sort of job placement program, so I called around to see what they had available.” Without creating an intensive, formula-filled spreadsheet, de la Osa relied on AI-generated research, iPhone notes and an Etsy-purchased template to keep track of medications and other care responsibilities, which aided in hiring and managing a nurse at $20 an hour. Compared to her former company-provided caregivers, de la Osa was able to pay a trained nurse $4 to $5 more an hour, while still saving $13 an hour for daily care. “It was pretty significant on both sides to offer the nursing student more and really get more,” she said. “It was really big to have somebody that could make somewhat informed decisions. Ultimately, within weeks of the nursing student starting, mom’s blood pressure kept going up. She was so calm, never rattled. She was able to keep me updated while I was working in an office and we agreed together when it was time to call 911. “There were scenarios with the other caregivers where I was calming them down because they had never been through something like that before,” de la Osa continued. “I didn’t have the space to freak out myself because I had to take care of mom and the caregiver, too. To have them add to the trauma by making it more chaotic was not a good experience. To have the contrast of a person with medical training walking me through the necessary steps was just what I needed.” De la Osa’s predicament is not unique. In fact, it is now the standard. According to a KPMG report released in March, while home health and personal care aides are the largest single occupation in the US economy, the industry is struggling to hire and retain its employees. The report, “Mapping the Care Economy in 2026,” found that “turnover is nearly 80%, several times higher than in other industries. Low pay, limited benefits and weak career ladders drive churn.” As a result, more family members are forced to become unpaid caregivers, find care that doesn’t quite hit the mark, or use assets and savings to afford professional care. “Everyone is trying to make it work for themselves,” said KPMG senior economist who researches the care economy and report author Matthew Nestler. “It’s almost a privatization of care. More and more people are experiencing this. When it comes to care and healthcare specifically, what you’re seeing is just a slow, steady growth of demand clashing with uneven or insufficient supply across an array of different care locations — whether in nursing homes, assisted living, or home healthcare — all of which have different structures, different payments.” Older Americans — namely baby boomers — are in the midst of retirement. The youngest boomers are 61, while the oldest members of the generation turn 80 this year. This is the largest generation in American history and it is currently in the middle of its peak, according to Nestler. In the early 2000s, economists pondered about what would happen to the workforce once baby boomers started to retire and now society is seeing an indelible, predictable population change. “People turn 65 every day and soon, the 85-plus population will double,” said Nestler. “With that, it means an increased demand for everything — aging, healthcare, consumer products. We’re facing a continuing growing demand for care with not enough supply and this is happening within the workforce because of low pay. What does that lead to? Empirical research tells us more informal caregiving, or family members providing more care because they can’t afford it or find it.” Not as easy as she thought While de la Osa found somewhat affordable care, her load didn’t disappear — it shifted. De la Osa, an only child, moved in 2020 from her Seattle, Washington, home to Detroit to be closer to care for her mother and father. Just months after her father passed away, her mother was in a car accident and required care so she and her mother moved in together. De la Osa then experienced the trauma of her mother, now 88, losing memories and becoming more frail by the day, she said. Because of the various medications her mother requires, she has been monitoring her blood pressure six times a day. “I had to make judgement calls on whether or not she should take a dose of meds because of her blood pressure. I thought, ‘This is way above my pay grade.’” When she found help through a company, she still found herself quite busy with caregiving duties, managing a rotating team of in-home health aids while building her own business. “I remember going into the office to work while having to talk to caregivers from there and having to manage that,” she said. “I never imagined caregiving — even of itself — was so much of a mental and emotional load. There’s them not understanding what to do, unable to keep track of everything. That was a mess. I was just so exhausted and feeling like even the most simple things were really hard.” A broken system While de la Osa had not previously considered a facility for her mother, the months of emotional hardship brought her to gather and hide assisted-living and nursing home folders in her car. To her surprise, after several 911 calls in a manner of weeks, de la Osa’s mother said, “I think it’s time,” signalling to her daughter that an assisted-living community was the next move. “I think a lot of times, people fight it,” said de la Osa. “If you couple the stubbornness of people who don’t want to go with the guilt of the person who knows that this is what’s best and safest for them, it’s not a good combination.” Her mother’s words were a relief. But the cost was burdensome. When she moved her mother into assisted living last July, she was told the renewal would increase by $1,300 more per month for just room and board. Shopping around, she noticed rates decreased by half the cost in lower-income counties. De la Osa found a new assisted living facility this year for her mother in Sterling Heights. With the rise in demand and growth of the aging population, another move may be in the near future.
