articles.title: Commentary: Treating homelessness as a crime doesn’t work
articles.description: Everyone deserves a safe place to live, but for many Michiganders, even full-time work doesn’t pay enough to afford basic needs, including housing. To address the homelessness resulting from this structural problem in the economy, some communities are misguidedly turning to the criminal legal system. We at the Michigan League for Public Policy urge them […]
articles.content: Man sleeping on the street outside the Fort Cass People Mover Station in Detroit, Michigan in June 2026 (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)Everyone deserves a safe place to live, but for many Michiganders, even full-time work doesn’t pay enough to afford basic needs, including housing. To address the homelessness resulting from this structural problem in the economy, some communities are misguidedly turning to the criminal legal system. We at the Michigan League for Public Policy urge them to focus on investments in affordable housing and supportive services rather than further punishing people our economy has left behind. To afford a two-bedroom apartment in Michigan, a full-time worker must earn $25.53 per hour – an increase of 47% over 2020. Meanwhile, the average renter wage remains under $20 per hour. And people earning the minimum wage must work 74 hours a week to cover rent and other basic living expenses. Being unable to afford a home shouldn’t be a crime, but our country has a long history of treating it that way. This approach has gained even more traction in recent years, even though it’s never proven effective in reducing homelessness. Owosso vigil honors two people found dead as residents raise concerns over homelessness In 2024, a U.S. Supreme Court decision gave local communities wide latitude to ticket and jail people who are unhoused, even when there isn’t shelter space for them. Since then, hundreds of cities, including five in Michigan, have passed laws further criminalizing survival activities by people who are homeless. Then came a presidential executive order conflating mental health disabilities with homelessness, and calling for the weakening of protections against involuntary commitment. The order also directs federal agencies to abandon humane, evidence-based practices and prioritize funding for communities that rely on the arrest and incarceration of people who are unhoused and disabled. But these crackdowns won’t reduce homelessness or make our communities safer, because they’re based on false stereotypes. Many people experiencing homelessness work despite facing barriers related to health, transportation and discrimination. Recent research shows that more than half of adults staying in homeless shelters and 40% of those who are unsheltered are formally employed. For many, job loss is what triggers a fall into homelessness. Forty percent of Michigan households struggle to pay for the basics. The U.S. doesn’t provide the same level of protection for workers and their wages that other well-resourced nations do, so when people get laid off or can’t work due to illness or injury, it can be catastrophic. Locking up people who are homeless doesn’t improve public safety, either. The overwhelming majority of crime is committed by people who actually have housing. Across the nation, people who are experiencing homelessness are known to account for less than 5% of jail bookings, and they’re far more likely to be the victim of a violent crime rather than the perpetrator. Here in Lansing, where the League is based, we’re seeing what happens when people are deemed unworthy of safety simply because they’re struggling to survive: five of our unhoused neighbors have died in less than a year. Homicide has been determined in three of these deaths and has not been ruled out for the other two. Lansing City Council hears calls for emergency homelessness response, delays action None of us should look away from homelessness or blame people who are unhoused for their plight. Homelessness is just the extreme endpoint of a convergence of broader social forces that is making life increasingly difficult for all but the wealthiest among us. People who are unhoused are not the reason our groceries, utilities, healthcare and housing are getting more expensive. They aren’t the reason the middle class is shrinking, or that families are falling further into debt and feeling more anxious about how they will live in retirement. We need to look to the corporate interests and policymakers who have built an economy that leaves so many families just one missed paycheck or unexpected expense away from losing their homes. Income inequality is growing, and today, the wealthiest 1% of Michigan households have incomes nearly 22 times greater than the bottom 99%. While we’re all spending more to put food on the table and fill our gas tanks, corporate profits are soaring. The world’s largest and most profitable corporations are paying workers poverty wages while their CEOs enjoy salaries hundreds of times higher. It’s time to stop punishing those with the least and focus on real solutions: worker empowerment, a robust social safety net and affordable housing for everyone. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

articles.title: Agent-to-agent communication: How AI agents work together
articles.description: Learn how agent-to-agent communication works, how the A2A protocol compares with MCP, and how AI agents delegate tasks and share context across systems.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Agent-to-agent communication is a structured process for AI agents to communicate and collaborate on requests from human users and systems. The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, also known as the agent-to-agent protocol, is the primary open standard for this operation. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a similar open standard, but designed for connecting AI agents to external tools and data repositories through a universal interface. MCP helps customer service agents access the knowledge bases, CRM systems, booking systems, and other tools necessary to facilitate front-line contacts. Agent-to-agent communication is a standardized method for AI agents to discover one another’s capabilities, delegate tasks, and exchange contexts and data for larger, ongoing, multi-step tasks. Its purpose is to facilitate AI agents coordinating among themselves without a human operator needing to shuttle workloads back and forth or attempting to force a generalist large language model (LLM) to process workloads that require enough specialized knowledge and concurrent activity to strain its context window. Open standards such as A2A and MCP help resolve two problems: siloed resources and the M x N bottleneck in systems integration. Agentic AI works best when you can configure agents to operate within a specific subdomain or scope of work. That helps keep their context window within manageable tolerances. However, that requires siloing them from each other, which means either relying on a human operator to facilitate communication between systems or relying on bespoke network integrations, which creates its own problem. The M x N problem arises when, without universal communication standards, M AI agents need N point-to-point APIs to external resources. Managing M x N brittle integrations at scale quickly becomes unsustainable. A viable agent-to-agent network needs to demonstrate four key capabilities: Multi-agent systems, where several specialized AI agents work together toward a shared goal, can exist in several topologies: centralized, hierarchical, decentralized, or sequential. A2A is the primary protocol for agent-to-agent communication in most of them, and MCP gives the agents access to tools and data. These topologies are explored in depth in our article, Multi-agent systems explained: How AI agents work together, but in brief, multi-agent systems operate in a plan-delegate-execute loop. Agentic AI is the approach to giving artificial intelligence agency. In other words, it lays out how AI can receive inputs, autonomously reason on them, and make decisions and execute actions. The goal is to enable autonomy over time, rather than autonomy to react to a single-turn prompt. An AI agent is a specific implementation of this approach. It’s a self-contained software system run by an underlying AI model that is capable of receiving inputs, reasoning and making decisions, and executing one or more tasks autonomously Conversational AI is an artificial intelligence system specialized in generating text or speech responses to prompts. For example, it can handle generative dialogues, transcriptions, sentiment matching, or information retrieval. Agentic AI may include conversational capabilities, but it is defined by its decision-making, problem-solving, and tool-execution capabilities. AI agents can often take deterministic system actions, such as executing a database query or scheduling an appointment in a calendar system. A conversational AI system on its own generates responses and does not take these actions unless it is built as an agent with access to tools, as voice agents in ElevenAgents are. Agent-to-agent communication occurs primarily through two open-standard protocols: Agent2Agent and Model Context Protocol. They aren’t competitors, they solve different problems. A2A connects agents to each other. MCP connects agents to tools. A2A and MCP are not the only protocols proposed for connecting agents. Others, such as IBM’s Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), have also appeared, and the space is still evolving. It’s possible to build AI agents using closed proprietary frameworks. You use one vendor’s SDKs, host on their infrastructure, and connect to other services within that “walled garden” using internal APIs. This model can work well in many use cases. However, as soon as you want your walled-off AI agent to communicate with any external agent or tool, you need to start writing bespoke APIs for them. In other words, you step into the M x N problem. Open standards help counteract that problem by acting as universal translators. They reduce vendor lock-in, which can limit your systems’ functionality. You gain the ability to build novel cross-organizational and cross-framework workflows. A2A is an open protocol originally developed by Google to allow AI agents to communicate directly with one another and delegate tasks. Agents don’t need to comprehend each other’s internal workings to communicate over A2A. It treats each agent as a black box (e.g., independent and opaque). A2A defines three actors: the user, the client agent, and the server (remote) agent. A user, whether a person or a system, submits a high-level request as a prompt to a client agent. That agent extracts intent and the final deliverables the user wants from the prompt, then parcels out sub-tasks that it and other agents can complete to achieve that goal. The client agent identifies which other remote agents, or server agents, can perform those sub-tasks by reading their advertised agent cards. An agent card is like a digital menu that advertises an agent’s identity, skills, hosting URL, and the modalities it can work with (e.g., text, audio, video, etc.). The client agent selects which server agents it needs to work with to complete the user’s high-level objectives and then structures tasks into A2A format for them, which includes four components: The server agent receives tasks via an HTTP endpoint at the URL on its agent card. It executes the task and returns the results along with any required artifacts in a return message. MCP is an open protocol developed by Anthropic to solve the M x N problem for agentic AI. It lets AI agents interact with external tools and data sources through a single, unified interface. An AI agent maintains a running MCP client that queries all connected MCP servers for a catalog of the services and data sources they offer on demand. The client has to authenticate with the server, which will only expose the services the client is authorized to use. When a user submits a request to the agent, it extracts the user’s intent and checks its training data and those MCP catalogs to decide how it can best complete their request. If it decides it needs access to tooling or data available via an MCP server, it sends a JSON-RPC request to the server, which returns a response that the AI agent ingests and uses to fulfill the user’s request. A2A and MCP solve different problems. They’re not mutually exclusive, with many teams using both in similar workflows. Delegating work between specialist agents Giving an agent access to a CRM, knowledge base, or calendar Not used. Native agent transfer and Workflows handle handoffs Supported as a hosted server and as a client When an AI agent makes an MCP tool call, there will be some degree of latency. That is usually tolerable to a user in a text chat interface, but even a short delay when talking to a conversational agent can disrupt the customer experience. Running conversational agents at enterprise scale requires backend MCP integration that can operate in near real time. MCP is one of several ways to connect ElevenAgents to your systems, alongside webhook tools, client tools, code tools, and system tools. Mid-conversation, agents can fetch key contextual information from your connected systems and take action without disrupting the conversational flow. ElevenLabs supports MCP in two deployment models: An ElevenAgents hosted MCP server allows you to have a natural language interface to your ElevenAgents workspace directly from Claude, Cursor, or ChatGPT. For example, you can ask Claude in natural language to build a new customer service agent that duplicates your production agent but uses a new voice model. Then deploy it to a test environment for your team to evaluate. ElevenAgents can also use MCP as a client. You can connect your ElevenAgents workspace to external MCP servers. For example, you can configure your new customer service agent with access to your CRM so it can look up important customer details during a live call. Then also connect it to your support technician calendaring system to schedule service calls for customers. ElevenAgents handles agent-to-agent handoffs natively rather than through the A2A protocol. Two features cover most multi-agent setups: To see how this orchestration works under the hood, read our guide to the ElevenAgents orchestration engine. Keeping agents focused on specialist tasks makes them work more reliably within better-defined context windows. This reduces the risk of hallucination, and more focused instructions can improve operational performance. Let’s consider an example of a front-line contact center agent handing off a customer to a specialist scheduling agent. ElevenAgents supports multi-agent collaboration through native agent transfer and Workflows, and connects to your tools through MCP as both a hosted server and a client. Get started with multi-agent Workflows and MCP-connected ElevenLabs agents today or learn more about ElevenAgents. Agent to agent refers to AI agents communicating and delegating tasks to one another directly, using standardized protocols such as A2A, without a human passing information between them. A client agent reads a remote agent’s agent card to learn its skills, then sends it a task. The remote agent runs the task and returns the result, along with any artifacts, in a message. A2A (Agent2Agent) is an open protocol that lets AI agents discover each other, delegate tasks, and exchange results. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that connects AI agents to external tools and data sources. A2A connects agents to other agents, while MCP connects agents to tools. Teams often use them together. Yes, AI agents can communicate with each other and delegate subtasks as part of larger, multi-step tasks using structured, open-standard communications protocols such as Agent2Agent (A2A). The Model Context Protocol (MCP) also allows agents to use tools and access data on external systems in a standardized interface. Modern AI agents carry out a number of important functions: Making an AI agent means creating an autonomous AI system for a specific function. The design occurs in three steps: Agentic AI is an approach to giving artificial intelligence agency to autonomously make decisions and carry out actions in the real world. An AI agent is a specific software implementation of agentic AI. Jack Limebear is on the Growth team, acting as a content writer and strategist across the blog and insights pages. articles.title: Webinar recap: Refresh your Black Friday ads with ElevenCreative
articles.description: Ad platforms now use your creative to find buyers. Here's how teams refresh, test, and localize ads every week through January.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. You put a lot into your Black Friday creative, and you want it to work as hard as possible. The question is how long it lasts. Ad platforms like Meta and Google now rely on the creative itself to find buyers, so the number of distinct ads a team can ship limits how much it can spend profitably. In a live workshop on refreshing ads for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, Gabe Michael, forward deployed creative at ElevenLabs, and Jan Emmanuele, deployment strategist at ElevenLabs, walked through why creative production is the bottleneck in peak season and what an always-on alternative looks like. This post covers what they shared and how to apply it between now and January. Targeting on ad platforms has become much broader. Instead of narrow audience settings doing the work, the platforms read the ad and decide who should see it. Ads that look and sound nearly the same get treated as a single idea, so 10 slight tweaks of one concept buy you very little new reach or insight. Winning ads are rare and hard to predict. A team shipping a few new ads each week waits a long time between winners, while a team shipping many more finds them far sooner. That's why the strongest brands test far more creative than everyone else, and why the winner is often an ad nobody on the team would have picked. Peak season compresses all of this. A large share of November and December online spend lands in the five days of Cyber Week, and every brand is bidding for the same shoppers in that window. Your top ads will get seen, but they'll get seen by the same people over and over. With each repeat view, someone who hasn't already converted is less likely to act. The weeks after launch are harder. Teams have to spot which ads are wearing out, replace them before results drop, and carry what worked into December and January. People respond better to ads in their own language. But many teams still run in only one language because each new language used to mean a new production cycle with its own budget and turnaround. As a result, brands either run their original-language ads globally and accept lower conversion rates in non-native markets, or they localize a handful of priority markets and ignore the long tail. Taking a winning ad into a new market is often cheaper than finding a new winner there. The traditional creative model runs in sequence: brand identity, creative strategy, production, distribution, then analysis at the end. Each step hands off to the next, and each handoff costs time many teams don't have during peak season. Adding AI usually replaces the production step with prompting, which speeds up one stage but keeps every handoff in place. Michael and Emmanuele described a different model, where agents run every step and the team directs the work as creative producers. That's how Ads Engine in ElevenCreative is built. It started as an internal workflow that the ElevenLabs paid marketing team built to localize ad campaigns across seven languages, and it's now available to every brand and agency. Scenario: The team wants to turn a live Black Friday static ad into more sizes, variants, and languages before it fatigues. Why it matters: Every variant in every language comes from one approved concept, without a new design or translation cycle for each. Scenario: The team wants to refresh a live video ad with new hooks and take it into new markets. Why it matters: Video is where most ad spend goes, and it's the hardest format to refresh because every change used to mean a reshoot or a re-edit. Changing the hook lets a team test the variant as a new idea, which stretches the life of a concept that already works. The first is giving the AI too little to work with. The team still has to define the goal of the ad and who it's for. With that in place, the tools multiply what the team can ship. The second is taking too little risk. Once the brand foundation is set, a long chain of briefs and approvals only slows the team down. Launch more variants, see what wins, then put budget behind the winners. The common thread is that a team's time should go into the original idea and the decisions about it. articles.title: Michigan state parks offer outdoor alternative to Black Friday craze
articles.description: Michigan previously offered free admission to state parks on Black Friday, but now more people get in with the annual pass.
articles.content: Hiking to the Little Sable Point Lighthouse at Silver Lake State Park.(Dustin Dwyer / Michigan Public)If the Black Friday shopping craze doesn’t appeal to you this year, here’s one alternative: go for a hike.The outdoor retailer REI kicked off a trend to “opt outside” on the busy shopping day by closing its doors in 2015. It gave its workers the day off, and encouraged customers to enjoy the outdoors rather than face the Black Friday shopping frenzy.The Michigan Department of Natural Resources encouraged the idea by offering free admission to state parks in 2018.“We haven’t done that for a while,” said Tom Bissett, chief of the DNR’s Parks and Recreation Division.As more people signed up for the annual state parks pass when they renewed their vehicle registration, Bissett said the idea of one free day was less relevant.“Rather than focusing on sort of a free day, or a free single admission day, we try to focus on the fact that realistically, for 15 bucks, you can use the parks all year round,” Bissett said.Black Friday is an ideal day to take advantage of the pass, Bissett said. He said a hike is a great post-Thanksgiving activity for families.“It’s also kind of a quieter time of the year to experience the state parks,” Bissett said. “So you might get to see a little bit more in the way of nature than you would in a normal day.”Weather could be an issue on Friday, so it may be a wet hike for those who decide to opt outside. But at least you can still avoid the crowds.“Some of Michigan’s best experiences that don’t require standing in line are at the Michigan state parks,” Bissett said. “So we’d love to see people come out.”

articles.title: Lawmakers are reaching across the aisle for Michigan’s trails system
articles.description: Spanning more than 13,000 miles across the state, Michigan’s trails system offers hikers, bikers, equestrians and snowmobilers plenty of space to blow off steam. While many know Michigan as the Great Lakes State, the state has earned another nickname – the Trails State – due to its extensive network of outdoor trails, which are maintained […]
articles.content: Multi-use trail in Sleepy Hollow State Park, DeWitt, Michigan (Photo by Susan J. Demas/Michigan Advance)Spanning more than 13,000 miles across the state, Michigan’s trails system offers hikers, bikers, equestrians and snowmobilers plenty of space to blow off steam. While many know Michigan as the Great Lakes State, the state has earned another nickname – the Trails State – due to its extensive network of outdoor trails, which are maintained in collaboration between state and local governments Brought together by a desire to promote and enhance the various trails crisscrossing the state, lawmakers in the Michigan House and Senate are reaching across the aisle to establish the Michigan Trails Caucus, chaired by Rep. Parker Fairbairn (R-Harbor Springs). Speaking with Michigan Advance, Fairbairn said he began talking with the state’s various trails groups in the wake of the 2025 ice storm, discussing the ways the storms impacted – and continue to impact – the trails system to this day. A common theme in these discussions is just how difficult it is to keep up with trail maintenance. “They only have so many volunteers. The equipment, in a lot of cases, is outdated and becoming obsolete if they’re not already. And you know, they receive money from the state to help manage the trails,” Fairbairn said. Grooming Michigan snowmobile trails. (Photo by Marla R. Miller/Michigan Advance) In these cases Fairbairn said money is often a real problem. In founding the caucus, he hoped to look through the Department of Natural Resources’ budget to see how funding for trails is being spent. However, the caucus’s purpose is twofold, Fairbairn said, with education on Michigan’s trails system serving as the other key focus. “My hope is we’ll have different organizations who work and deal with the trails come in and present to the caucus or present to other people interested in trails and educate them on issues that snowmobile groups are having and issues that these bike groups are having,” Fairbairn said. As of Nov. 17, Fairbairn said the caucus had 25 members. While the caucus won’t be able to address every issue, members will at least be educated on the importance of Michigan’s trails and how various organizations are helping them, Fairbairn said. Trails leading out from Oval Beach in Saugatuck, Michigan on Aug. 21, 2024. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance) In a statement to the Advance, Rep. Will Snyder (D-Muskegon), one of the caucus’s vice chairs, pointed to the state’s trails as a great resource for residents, as well as a draw for tourists. “As a legislator, I’ve been a champion for expanding tourism opportunities, and supporting our trails system is another way of bolstering tourism in Michigan,” Snyder said. “In the Muskegon area, we’ve been working with Laketon and Fruitland townships on a trail system expansion that would connect local trails to the Fred Meijer Berry Junction Trail, which, in turn, is tied together with most other regional West Michigan trails.” While Snyder did not anticipate much action in the Legislature during the lame duck period that follows the election, he said the caucus would continue to grow its ranks and develop its vision for the state’s trails in the next legislative session beginning in 2027.

Michigan economic development agency finds replacement for expired business grant program
articles.description: A new grant program is working to attract more business investment to Michigan. The MiGrow program will cover up to a quarter of a new project’s costs, with a maximum award of $1 million.
articles.content: A sign reading "now hiring" stands outside a Grand Rapids business.(Brett Dahlberg / Michigan Public )Michigan is trying a new tool to attract business investment.The Michigan Economic Development Corporation approved a new grant program this month to help with project costs like buying land, equipment, and technology.To be eligible for MiGROW grants, businesses must pay at least 75% of new workers the regional median wage or more. The number of new jobs has to equal at least 1% of what’s already available in the county.The grants program will cover up to a quarter of a new project’s costs, with a maximum award of $1 million.MEDC spokesperson Michelle Grinnell said inflation and higher business costs can sometimes create a “gap” that can block companies from growing in Michigan.“If there’s a great company that wants to expand in a community here in Michigan but there is a barrier to doing that, or it will cost them less money to do a similar expansion at a facility in a different state, this grant helps ensure that we can keep that investment and those jobs here in Michigan,” Grinnell said.The new MiGROW grants are replacing the expired Michigan Business Development Program. That program, which had a maximum award of $10 million, expired at the end of September. State lawmakers didn’t set aside money to continue it.Grinnell maintains the business development program was successful. A report from Fiscal Year 2025 suggests the projects it sponsored had created 7,955 permanent jobs at that point.MiGrow comes at a time when lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle have become skeptical of business incentives. Critics have argued the state shouldn’t be paying private businesses to build here.Grinnell said MiGROW meets the current moment.“We’ve really leaned into the mandate that we have heard loud and clear to support Michigan, and small businesses and Michigan businesses across the state, and it is also sized appropriately to the funding that we were appropriated from our policymakers for the fiscal year,” she said.The grants will prioritize projects in industries like manufacturing, engineering, and energy.Grinnell said a regional approach will also help projects get buy-in from local communities. Previous MEDC grant recipients like a failed battery plant in Mecosta County got significant local pushback.Grinnell said the state will claw back any money it spends on projects that don’t follow through on their requirements.“We know that the vast majority of projects are successful. The projects that do not move forward are the exception to the rule. But we have built in the performance in this to ensure that the taxpayer dollars are protected,” she said.

articles.title: Michigan retailers optimistic going into holiday shopping season
articles.description: A new survey shows, despite a slow start, Michigan retailers are seeing an increase in sales going into the heart of the holiday shopping season.
articles.content: Michigan retailers are optimistic going into the 2026 holiday shopping season.(Jelena Danilovic/Jelena - stock.adobe.com / 178568794)A new survey shows, despite a slow start, Michigan retailers are seeing an increase in sales going into the heart of the holiday shopping season. Vic Veda, Vice President of Communications at the Michigan Retailers Association, said retail sales are picking up after a sluggish September and improving October. She said a growing number of holiday shoppers are looking to give something different.“27% of shoppers are looking for some sort of experience to gift," Veda said. "And that’s up from 19% about five years ago. But these types of gifts are very popular among Gen Z."Experiential gift ideas include salon gift cards and family escape room trips.Veda also said the MRA's survey shows some shoppers are moving away from buying gifts online, though more than half of holiday shoppers surveyed say they plan to shop online.Retailers are also optimistic this holiday season; in the survey, 59% of retailers predicted their sales would increase, while 25% anticipate their sales to decline, the MRA said.The National Retail Federation predicts retail sales in November and December will grow 4.2% over 2025, the MRA said.

articles.content: Volvo provided flights from Washington, DC, to Copenhagen, Denmark, and accommodation so Ars could drive the XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. COPENHAGEN, Denmark—If we lived in the world that Volvo’s product planners expected back when the current XC90 debuted in 2015, both it and the smaller but related XC60 (which arrived in 2017) might have been the last of their kind as everything went electric. As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in the critically important US market. At the same time, Europe and China are electrifying, which seems like an argument against spending resources on developing all-new replacements for models that might not have an eight-year lifespan in most markets. So instead, Volvo has given the XC60 and XC90 another lifecycle refresh. The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. And that’s no bad thing—both were, and remain, handsome shapes that are popular with Volvo’s customer base. Instead, the Swedish automaker’s attention has been on bringing the technology up to date for model year 2028 standards. Which means a much bigger battery for the PHEVs, with sufficient capacity for a couple of days of daily driving for most of us before needing to be recharged. There’s also new, modern infotainment and interiors that are now even nicer to spend time in than before.Read full article Comments

articles.title: How Serbia’s students devised a winning strategy to bring down strongman Vucic
articles.description: How Serbia’s students devised a winning strategy to bring down strongman Vucic AP News Serbia's new student-led government proposes a 4-day work week and no reality TV until 11 p.m. CBS News Serbia's student movement yet to name prime minister as deadlines loom Reuters How We Defeated a Color Revolution: Serbia’s Direct-Democratic Student Movement Against Goliath CounterPunch.org Serbia Students WV News
articles.content: BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Marko Bojovic got up early on the day of Serbia’s parliamentary election last month. As a logistics coordinator for the student movement, he wanted one final look at a plan designed to make sure activists were safe and the ballot was not rigged. The meticulously crafted plan relied on a network of some 60,000 volunteers with specialized mobile teams that communicated through dedicated phone apps and kept changing venues to avoid state surveillance and stay connected, he said. After all, the grassroots movement was taking on a formidable opponent. Strongman ruler Aleksandar Vucic was in power for 14 years, equipped with a well-oiled electoral machine, seemingly unlimited resources, a state apparatus, and almost the entire media landscape under the control of his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party. Nonetheless, 24-year-old Bojovic was confident that the Students List would succeed. After leading two years of protests, the students managed nationwide mobilization, flawless organization, and — crucially — empathy. Bojovic, who has a degree in history, drew a comparison between the election showdown and a Spartan battle. ”We would either come back with our shields, or on them,” he said. Their preparations paid off. Serbia’s youth on Oct. 25 scored a stunning victory admired well beyond the Balkan country’s borders. A month later, Bojovic and another logistics team member, Adrian Kraljevic, spoke to the AP about the strategy that helped undermine Vucic’s popularity and defeat his party by a landslide. The students’ protests demanding accountability over the November 2024 train station tragedy in Serbia’s north resonated among the voters hungry for justice and equality after decades of crisis and corruption. The canopy collapse at the Novi Sad train station killed 16 people, and many in Serbia were convinced that shoddy renovation work tainted by graft and negligence was to blame. Djordje Trikos, a London-based political campaign strategist, said the disaster acted as a catalyst for change. “This is where they started thinking: ‘I have nothing to lose if I change my vote,’” Trikos said. “Many people switched sides not because they necessarily believed the students were the better alternative, but because they considered the reality they lived in unbearable.” Bojovic said the students realized Vucic’s system was a “pyramid” and that the way was to dismantle the base and work upwards. To achieve this, activists launched a “student in every village” campaign, marching and cycling through the country to reach Vucic’s strongholds. “We knocked on almost every door in Serbia,” he said. It wasn’t easy. Pro-government media and officials, including Vucic himself, repeatedly attacked the students as enemies of the state who wanted to destroy the country under orders from abroad. The students, Bojovic said, countered by showing the citizens that “we are their children.” Dragica Jovanovic, an 83-year-old pensioner from Belgrade, said it worked. Though she “liked our president (Vucic) very much ... the students touched my heart,” Jovanovic said. Vucic, she added, “made me choose between him and my grandchildren.” The next step was to involve volunteers from all backgrounds at every stage of the election. Most were trained as polling-station observers, ballot counters, security staff, or call-center operators, Bojovic said. With their resolve and youth, the students won the hearts and minds of many Serbians who were fed up with both Vucic’s SNS and the other established parties. The students vowed to restore democracy and fight corruption, while avoiding divisive topics such as relations with Russia or the European Union. Trikos drew a comparison with Hungary, whose authoritarian ex-Prime Minister Viktor Orban was swept from power in a similar way in April. Both Hungary and Serbia, Trikos said, were governed by leaders with nearly 15 years in office who had faced a changed electorate, an aging base, and young voters who wanted to change the system. “So, it’s not only the students and their, say, creative genius or plan that contributed to these results,” he said. “This is almost like a rule across all democracies: young voters tend to vote anti-establishment, and if you are in power for 15 years, they will naturally perceive you as the establishment.” Two rounds of local elections in 2025 and 2026 helped shape the students’ strategy for the crucial vote in October. Those earlier ballots were marred by reports of pro-government supporters attacking election monitors, students and journalists. Bojovic said that students “took a beating but the regime has shown its cards.” Kraljevic, who is 21, added that the students realized “we need to know where our people are in real time so that we could help them if they are in danger or get hurt.” The solution was a set of special apps, created with the help of Serbia’s inventive IT community, Kraljevic said. The apps — which were turned off after the Oct. 25 vote — were designed to track mobile election teams and serve as tools of communication that creators hoped could not be traced or monitored by the authorities. The apps were protected by multiple security layers and hosted on Android and iOS stores under cryptic names, Kraljevic said. Volunteers at the parliamentary ballot received their usernames and security codes to activate them on election day, he added. Each of the apps, Kraljevic said, featured three core tools: a team-tracking map, a live communication panel and a panic button so that anyone in danger could send an immediate call for help — which thankfully wasn’t widely used. Multiple apps compartmentalized risk — if one group was compromised, the rest of the groups could continue without jeopardizing the entire operation of several thousand people, he explained. Local and international digital watchdog groups said they have evidence that the phone of the Belgrade university rector was infected with spyware, along with the phones of several students, activists and a prosecutor. The spyware included both Israeli NSO Group’s Pegasus and domestically developed malware, the report said. Separately, some students said they noticed people watching them, or saw the content of their meetings popping up in pro-government tabloids. Bojovic said the students changed venues for meetings to avoid surveillance, and were “constantly on the move,” going through “every basement, every attic, and countless cafes.” Serbia’s Security Information Agency, or BIA, has dismissed allegations as “false and malicious” and aimed at fueling instability. Balloting raised hope for the students from early hours on Oct. 25. with people lining up for hours in a joyful atmosphere. But as the day drew to a close, tensions began to rise. Special police were deployed in central Belgrade, fencing off streets. Vucic’s masked and hooded loyalists started converging in a park near Parliament where they had been camping for over a year, and from where they had repeatedly attacked journalists and activists. Kraljevic said masked men lined up in front of his polling station, and “it was very tense.” But as Vucic conceded defeat at 9.30 p.m., the group “quietly dispersed,” he said. Hundreds of thousands of people soon flooded the streets in an outburst of spontaneous celebration. For Bojovic and Kraljevic, the election victory meant a return to their everyday lives before the protests. Kraljevic said he is happy that “my mother can finally say my name over the phone.” Previously, he said, she was afraid that he would be followed and come to harm. Now her anxiety has lifted. AP Writer Jovana Gec contributed to this report.
